titleStmt.title: On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies
titleStmt.author: Albert Einstein

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: On the Electrodynamics of Moving Bodies

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: The kinematics of the rigid body, and the relationships between rigid bodies, clocks and electromagnetic processes on which any theory of the electrodynamics of moving bodies rests.
span.quote: The theory to be developed is based—like all electrodynamics—on the kinematics of the rigid body, since the assertions of any such theory have to do with the relationships between rigid bodies (systems of co-ordinates), clocks, and electromagnetic processes.

span.label: Why does Maxwell's electrodynamics, applied to moving bodies, lead to asymmetries which do not appear to be inherent in the phenomena?
span.quote: It is known that Maxwell's electrodynamics—as usually understood at the present time—when applied to moving bodies, leads to asymmetries which do not appear to be inherent in the phenomena.

span.label: Shows that two postulates - the principle of relativity and the constancy of the velocity of light - suffice for a consistent electrodynamics of moving bodies, making a luminiferous ether superfluous.
span.quote: These two postulates suffice for the attainment of a simple and consistent theory of the electrodynamics of moving bodies based on Maxwell's theory for stationary bodies. The introduction of a “luminiferous ether” will prove to be superfluous

span.label: prediction
span.quote: We will now enumerate the properties of the motion of the electron which result from the system of equations (A) , and are accessible to experiment.

span.label: relativity of simultaneity: two events simultaneous in one frame are not simultaneous in another moving relative to it
span.quote: So we see that we cannot attach any absolute signification to the concept of simultaneity, but that two events which, viewed from a system of co-ordinates, are simultaneous, can no longer be looked upon as simultaneous events when envisaged from a system which is in motion relatively to that system.

span.label: theory
span.quote: We will raise this conjecture (the purport of which will hereafter be called the “Principle of Relativity”) to the status of a postulate, and also introduce another postulate, which is only apparently irreconcilable with the former, namely, that light is always propagated in empty space with a definite velocity c which is independent of the state of motion of the emitting body.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A CONJECTURE IS RAISED TO THE STATUS OF A POSTULATE BY DECLARATION, AND NAMED IN THE SAME SENTENCE: the epistemic status of the claim is changed by an act of writing rather than by evidence, and the name it will carry hereafter is fixed in the same breath. A second postulate is introduced alongside it and described as ONLY APPARENTLY irreconcilable with the first
span.quote: We will raise this conjecture (the purport of which will hereafter be called the “Principle of Relativity”) to the status of a postulate, and also introduce another postulate, which is only apparently irreconcilable with the former, namely, that light is always propagated in empty space with a definite velocity c which is independent of the state of motion of the emitting body.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AN ENTITY IS DECLARED SUPERFLUOUS RATHER THAN REFUTED: the luminiferous ether is not argued to be absent but shown to be unnecessary, because the view to be developed will not require an absolutely stationary space provided with special properties, nor assign a velocity-vector to a point of empty space
span.quote: The introduction of a “luminiferous ether” will prove to be superfluous inasmuch as the view here to be developed will not require an “absolutely stationary space” provided with special properties, nor assign a velocity-vector to a point of the empty space in which electromagnetic processes take place.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A TERM IS COINED EXPRESSLY TO MAKE A VERBAL DISTINCTION, AND THE STATED PURPOSE IS PRESENTATIONAL: the coordinate system is called the stationary system in order to render the presentation more precise and to distinguish it VERBALLY from others that will be introduced later
span.quote: In order to render our presentation more precise and to distinguish this system of co-ordinates verbally from others which will be introduced hereafter, we call it the “stationary system.”

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A COMMON TERM CANNOT BE DEFINED AT ALL WITHOUT A STIPULATION, AND THE PAPER NAMES WHICH PART IS STIPULATED: an A-time and a B-time have been defined, but a common time for A and B CANNOT BE DEFINED AT ALL unless it is established BY DEFINITION that light takes the same time from A to B as from B to A. The equality is established, not measured
span.quote: We have so far defined only an “A time” and a “B time.” We have not defined a common “time” for A and B, for the latter cannot be defined at all unless we establish by definition that the “time” required by light to travel from A to B equals the “time” it requires to travel from B to A.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE PROPERTIES THE DEFINITION NEEDS ARE ASSUMED, NOT DERIVED: that the definition of synchronism is free from contradictions and possible for any number of points is ASSUMED, and so are the two relations quoted - the symmetry of synchrony and its transitivity - which are stated as universally valid rather than shown
span.quote: We assume that this definition of synchronism is free from contradictions, and possible for any number of points; and that the following relations are universally valid:— If the clock at B synchronizes with the clock at A, the clock at A synchronizes with the clock at B. If the clock at A synchronizes with the clock at B and also with the clock at C, the clocks at B and C also synchronize with each other.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A DEFINITION IS DECLARED SATISFACTORY AT ONE SCOPE AND UNSATISFACTORY AT ANOTHER, WITH BOTH SCOPES NAMED: substituting the position of a watch's hand for time works when defining a time exclusively for the place where the watch is, and stops working as soon as events at different places must be put in one series. The word does not fail - it fails OUTSIDE A STATED RANGE
span.quote: It might appear possible to overcome all the difficulties attending the definition of “time” by substituting “the position of the small hand of my watch” for “time.” And in fact such a definition is satisfactory when we are concerned with defining a time exclusively for the place where the watch is located; but it is no longer satisfactory when we have to connect in time series of events occurring at different places, or—what comes to the same thing—to evaluate the times of events occurring at places remote from the watch.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: ONE WORD IS GIVEN TO TWO DIFFERENT OPERATIONS AND THE PAPER'S RESULT IS THAT THEY DISAGREE: two measuring procedures are set out, the outcome of each is called THE LENGTH OF THE ROD, and they are told apart only by a trailing qualifier - in the moving system, in the stationary system - after which the text states plainly that the second differs from the first
span.quote: In accordance with the principle of relativity the length to be discovered by the operation ( a )—we will call it “the length of the rod in the moving system”—must be equal to the length l of the stationary rod. The length to be discovered by the operation ( b ) we will call “the length of the (moving) rod in the stationary system.” This we shall determine on the basis of our two principles, and we shall find that it differs from l .

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE PREVIOUS THEORY'S ASSUMPTION IS MADE VISIBLE BY BEING NAMED AS TACIT: current kinematics is said to assume TACITLY that the two operations give precisely equal lengths, and the assumption is then restated in other words - that a moving rigid body may be perfectly represented by the same body at rest
span.quote: Current kinematics tacitly assumes that the lengths determined by these two operations are precisely equal, or in other words, that a moving rigid body at the epoch t may in geometrical respects be perfectly represented by the same body at rest in a definite position.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: TWO SETS OF OBSERVERS APPLY THE SAME STATED CRITERION AND REACH OPPOSITE VERDICTS: one finds the clocks not synchronous while the other DECLARES them synchronous, from which the paper concludes that no ABSOLUTE SIGNIFICATION can be attached to the concept of simultaneity. The concept survives and loses its claim to hold independently of a frame
span.quote: Observers moving with the moving rod would thus find that the two clocks were not synchronous, while observers in the stationary system would declare the clocks to be synchronous. So we see that we cannot attach any absolute signification to the concept of simultaneity, but that two events which, viewed from a system of co-ordinates, are simultaneous, can no longer be looked upon as simultaneous events when envisaged from a system which is in motion relatively to that system.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: THE SAME EQUATIONS ARE CLOTHED IN WORDS TWICE AND THE TWO READINGS ARE LABELLED BY THEIR ERA: identical mathematics is given an OLD MANNER OF EXPRESSION, in which a moving charge feels an extra electromotive force, and a NEW MANNER OF EXPRESSION, in which it feels the electric force found by transforming to its own rest frame. THE CONTENT IS ONE AND THE VOCABULARY IS TWO, and the paper marks the difference as historical rather than factual
span.quote: Consequently the first three equations above allow themselves to be clothed in words in the two following ways:— If a unit electric point charge is in motion in an electromagnetic field, there acts upon it, in addition to the electric force, an “electromotive force” which, if we neglect the terms multiplied by the second and higher powers of v / c , is equal to the vector-product of the velocity of the charge and the magnetic force, divided by the velocity of light. (Old manner of expression.) If a unit electric point charge is in motion in an electromagnetic field, the force acting upon it is equal to the electric force which is present at the locality of the charge, and which we ascertain by transformation of the field to a system of co-ordinates at rest relatively to the electrical charge. (New manner of expression.) The analogy holds with “magnetomotive forces.”

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A CONCEPT IS DEMOTED TO AN AUXILIARY THAT OWES ITS EXISTENCE TO THE DESCRIPTION FRAME: electromotive force is said to play MERELY the part of an auxiliary concept, which OWES ITS INTRODUCTION to the circumstance that electric and magnetic forces do not exist independently of the state of motion of the coordinate system. The term is explained by the bookkeeping, not by the world
span.quote: We see that electromotive force plays in the developed theory merely the part of an auxiliary concept, which owes its introduction to the circumstance that electric and magnetic forces do not exist independently of the state of motion of the system of co-ordinates.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A CLASS OF QUESTIONS IS DISSOLVED RATHER THAN ANSWERED: the asymmetry the paper opened with is said to DISAPPEAR, and questions as to the SEAT of electrodynamic electromotive forces in unipolar machines are said to NOW HAVE NO POINT - retired without being settled either way
span.quote: Furthermore it is clear that the asymmetry mentioned in the introduction as arising when we consider the currents produced by the relative motion of a magnet and a conductor, now disappears. Moreover, questions as to the “seat” of electrodynamic electromotive forces (unipolar machines) now have no point.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: A DEFINITION IS CRITICISED AS NOT ADVANTAGEOUS RATHER THAN WRONG, AND THE CRITERION IS SIMPLICITY OF THE RESULTING LAWS: a footnote records that the definition of force given here is not advantageous, as Planck first showed, and that it is more to the point to define force so that the laws of momentum and energy take their simplest form. THE GROUND FOR PREFERRING ONE DEFINITION IS WHAT IT DOES TO THE REST OF THE THEORY
span.quote: The definition of force here given is not advantageous, as was first shown by M. Planck. It is more to the point to define force in such a way that the laws of momentum and energy assume the simplest form.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: AN INEXACTITUDE IN THE CENTRAL CONCEPT IS ACKNOWLEDGED AND EXPRESSLY NOT DISCUSSED: a footnote says an inexactitude LURKS in the concept of simultaneity of two events at approximately the same place and can only be removed by an abstraction - and then declines to take it up. The residue is named, located, and left
span.quote: We shall not here discuss the inexactitude which lurks in the concept of simultaneity of two events at approximately the same place, which can only be removed by an abstraction.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: NOT EINSTEIN'S VOICE - THE 1999 EDITION'S OWN NOTE. THE MOST FAMOUS SYMBOL IN THE THEORY IS NOT THE AUTHOR'S: the note records that the 1923 English translation modified Einstein's notation to conform to that in use by the 1920s, and that `c` for the speed of light replaced the `V` he actually wrote in 1905
span.quote: The 1923 English translation modified the notation used in Einstein's 1905 paper to conform to that in use by the 1920s; for example, c denotes the speed of light, as opposed the V used by Einstein in 1905.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: NOT EINSTEIN'S VOICE - THE 1999 EDITION'S OWN NOTE. A SYMBOL COLLISION WAS INTRODUCED BY TRANSLATION: the moving system's coordinates were introduced in the original paper WITHOUT BEING EXPLICITLY DEFINED, the 1923 translation used (X, Y, Z) for them, and the note says this CREATED AN AMBIGUITY between the X co-ordinates of the fixed system and the parallel axis of the moving one
span.quote: for the co-ordinates of the moving system k were introduced without explicitly defining them. In the 1923 English translation, (X, Y, Z) were used, creating an ambiguity between X co-ordinates in the fixed system K and the parallel axis in moving system k .

span.label: The theory declares its own domain: above the speed of light the deliberations are said to be meaningless, so nothing in the paper is offered about that regime.
span.quote: For velocities greater than that of light our deliberations become meaningless; we shall, however, find in what follows, that the velocity of light in our theory plays the part, physically, of an infinitely great velocity.

span.label: A known inexactitude in the concept of simultaneity is named and explicitly not discussed; the paper states it can only be removed by an abstraction.
span.quote: We shall not here discuss the inexactitude which lurks in the concept of simultaneity of two events at approximately the same place, which can only be removed by an abstraction.

span.label: The consistency of the synchronism definition is assumed, not proved.
span.quote: We assume that this definition of synchronism is free from contradictions, and possible for any number of points; and that the following relations are universally valid:—

span.label: The extension of the clock result from a polygonal path to a continuous curve is flagged in the text as an assumption.
span.quote: If we assume that the result proved for a polygonal line is also valid for a continuously curved line, we arrive at this result:

span.label: The classical composition of velocities is retained only as a first approximation.
span.quote: Thus the law of the parallelogram of velocities is valid according to our theory only to a first approximation.

span.label: The mass values derived are stated to depend on the definitions of force and acceleration chosen, with an explicit warning about comparing theories of the electron's motion.
span.quote: With a different definition of force and acceleration we should naturally obtain other values for the masses. This shows us that in comparing different theories of the motion of the electron we must proceed very cautiously.

span.label: A footnote records that the paper's own definition of force is not the advantageous one, crediting Planck.
span.quote: The definition of force here given is not advantageous, as was first shown by M. Planck. It is more to the point to define force in such a way that the laws of momentum and energy assume the simplest form.

span.label: A pendulum-clock is explicitly excluded from the clock comparison, because it is physically a system to which the Earth belongs.
span.quote: Not a pendulum-clock, which is physically a system to which the Earth belongs. This case had to be excluded.

span.label: The paper records that Lorentz's preceding memoir was not known to the author at the time, bounding what the work can be read as responding to.
span.quote: The preceding memoir by Lorentz was not at this time known to the author.

span.label: Provenance, not argument: the edition staged here silently corrects the 1923 translation, so a quote is verbatim in this edition and not necessarily in the published translation.
span.quote: In the original 1923 English edition, this phrase was erroneously translated as “plain figures”. I have used the correct “plane figures” in this document.

span.label: Provenance: the edition also corrects an equation that was wrong in Einstein's original paper, so the staged text differs from the 1905 original as well as from the 1923 translation.
span.quote: This equation was incorrectly given in Einstein's original paper and the 1923 English translation as

span.label: simultaneity
span.quote: So we see that we cannot attach any absolute signification to the concept of simultaneity

span.label: Principle of Relativity
span.quote: We will raise this conjecture (the purport of which will hereafter be called the “Principle of Relativity”) to the status of a postulate

span.label: postulate
span.quote: and also introduce another postulate, which is only apparently irreconcilable with the former

span.label: luminiferous ether
span.quote: The introduction of a “luminiferous ether” will prove to be superfluous

span.label: absolutely stationary space
span.quote: the view here to be developed will not require an “absolutely stationary space” provided with special properties

span.label: synchronous stationary clocks
span.quote: Thus with the help of certain imaginary physical experiments we have settled what is to be understood by synchronous stationary clocks located at different places

span.label: electromotive force
span.quote: We see that electromotive force plays in the developed theory merely the part of an auxiliary concept

span.label: auxiliary concept
span.quote: which owes its introduction to the circumstance that electric and magnetic forces do not exist independently of the state of motion of the system of co-ordinates

span.label: mass of the moving electron
span.quote: Taking the ordinary point of view we now inquire as to the “longitudinal” and the “transverse” mass of the moving electron.

span.label: definition of force
span.quote: The definition of force here given is not advantageous, as was first shown by M. Planck.

span.label: time - the reading of one clock, defined only for the place that clock occupies
span.quote: And in fact such a definition is satisfactory when we are concerned with defining a time exclusively for the place where the watch is located; but it is no longer satisfactory when we have to connect in time series of events occurring at different places

span.label: time - a quantity common to two distant places, which the paper says cannot be defined at all except by stipulation about light travel
span.quote: We have not defined a common “time” for A and B, for the latter cannot be defined at all unless we establish by definition that the “time” required by light to travel from A to B equals the “time” it requires to travel from B to A.

span.label: time of the stationary system - the frame-tied sense the paper adopts as its own reference
span.quote: It is essential to have time defined by means of stationary clocks in the stationary system, and the time now defined being appropriate to the stationary system we call it “the time of the stationary system.”

span.label: mass - longitudinal and transverse, two distinct masses the paper names for one moving electron
span.quote: Taking the ordinary point of view we now inquire as to the “longitudinal” and the “transverse” mass of the moving electron.

span.label: electromotive force - an auxiliary concept only, whose apparent existence tracks the frame of reference rather than a physical fact
span.quote: We see that electromotive force plays in the developed theory merely the part of an auxiliary concept, which owes its introduction to the circumstance that electric and magnetic forces do not exist independently of the state of motion of the system of co-ordinates.

span.label: Principle of Relativity —is-a→ postulate
span.quote: We will raise this conjecture (the purport of which will hereafter be called the “Principle of Relativity”) to the status of a postulate

span.label: luminiferous ether —same-as→ absolutely stationary space
span.quote: The introduction of a “luminiferous ether” will prove to be superfluous inasmuch as the view here to be developed will not require an “absolutely stationary space” provided with special properties

span.label: simultaneity —operationalised-as→ synchronous stationary clocks
span.quote: Thus with the help of certain imaginary physical experiments we have settled what is to be understood by synchronous stationary clocks located at different places, and have evidently obtained a definition of “simultaneous,” or “synchronous,” and of “time.”

span.label: mass of the moving electron —operationalised-as→ definition of force
span.quote: With a different definition of force and acceleration we should naturally obtain other values for the masses.

span.label: electromotive force —is-a→ auxiliary concept
span.quote: We see that electromotive force plays in the developed theory merely the part of an auxiliary concept, which owes its introduction to the circumstance that electric and magnetic forces do not exist independently of the state of motion of the system of co-ordinates.
